fatal_errors: The proposed entropy-stabilization mechanism is opposite to the target finding that active, non-sluggish diffusion and surface-energy-driven Au/Cu segregation govern stability.

It predicts stability throughout 473–1923 K without specifying composition, particle size, morphology, atmosphere, dwell time, or reaction environment, although these variables strongly control nanoparticle stability.

The cited evidence supports entropy stabilization only as a possible, composition-dependent tendency and does not justify universal stability up to 1923 K; E2 explicitly notes that ordering enthalpy can overcome entropy.
The hypothesis omits the experimentally relevant failure boundary near 673 K and the segregation, melting, evaporation, reshaping, and loss of small particles.

The proposed high-versus-low configurational-entropy comparison changes composition and likely surface energies simultaneously, so it cannot cleanly distinguish entropy stabilization from surface-energy-controlled kinetics.
explanation: The response recognizes the general HEA stability question and offers a nominally testable comparison, but mostly restates the conventional high-configurational-entropy baseline that the target study contradicts. It does not reconstruct the AuCoCuNiPt sub-10 nm system, staged vacuum heating to 973 K, or the coupled STEM-EDS and molecular-dynamics analysis. Its mechanism and predicted outcome disagree directly with the observed Au/Cu surface segregation, active diffusion, shape evolution, evaporation, particle loss, and 22% size reduction. The evidence establishes that some HEA nanoparticles can retain solid-solution structures over narrower temperature intervals, but it cannot support the blanket claim of stability across 473–1923 K. The falsification experiment has some value, yet requires controls that independently vary configurational entropy while matching composition-dependent surface energies, particle size, morphology, and environment.
